text: A few weeks later Haskett asked to speak with Waythorn, and in his mild, apologetic way he complained that Lilys French governess was not a proper influence. <break time="0.8s" /> By the decree of the courts I am entitled to have a voice in Lilys bringing up, he said quietly, and Waythorn could not deny that he was right. <break time="0.8s" /> In the course of the talk, it came out that Alice had seen Haskett after his first visit, although she had denied it when her husband asked her. <break time="0.8s" /> The governess was dismissed, and Waythorn, who had once thought of Haskett as a mere shadow from the past, now saw him as a man with real rights in his home. <break time="0.8s" /> At the same time his business with Varick drew the two men together so often that they began to greet each other almost like old acquaintances. <break time="0.8s" /> Once, at a ball, he saw Alice chatting easily with Varick, as calm as if a divorce were no more serious than a change of address. <break time="0.8s" /> It struck him that his wife was as easy as an old shoe, but a shoe that too many feet had worn into its comfortable shape. <break time="0.8s" /> Her ease, he realized, was the result of having adapted herself to so many people that she no longer had any sharp edges left. <break time="0.8s" /> Never had Waythorn felt so uncertain whether he admired her for this gift or pitied her for the price that she must have paid for it.
